endorsed.title: run_or_prewarm is a 700-line mega-function disguised as two public commands
endorsed.symptom: assistant_send and assistant_prewarm are thin shims that both immediately delegate to run_or_prewarm (lines 525-529, 582-586). run_or_prewarm is ~740 lines doing: session-id validation, prompt-size caps, config load, model resolution, Fable/Haiku kill-switch guards, effort resolution, permission-mode resolution, workspace root resolution (5-way priority), scratch-dir fallback, session-cwd pinning, session-model pinning, trust resolution, MCP config file provisioning, addendum selection, full-config flag computation, attachment validation, CLI-caps probe (spawn_blocking), CLI-version floor check, command object construction with 15+ args/flags, nothink-shim wiring (two branches), effort flag mapping, SpawnKey assembly, and finally the prewarm-or-dispatch branch. There are zero sub-function calls for any of these phases — it's a sequential monolith. The single conceptual seam — 'resolve everything needed to describe a spawn, then actually spawn' — is invisible in the code. Reading this fn to understand any one concern means skimming all the others.
endorsed.recommendation: Extract a SpawnParams struct (model, effort_level, permission_mode, use_full_config, use_api_key, trust_level, roots, addendum, caps, mcp_config_path, user_line, key, cmd) and a resolve_spawn_params(app, cfg, session_id, ...) -> Result<SpawnParams> function covering everything from config-load through key assembly. run_or_prewarm becomes: validate → resolve_spawn_params → if prewarm { prewarm_spawn } else { dispatch_turn }. This is a single internal refactor (no public API changes), reduces the fn to ~80 lines, and lets you read the resolution logic in isolation. Not a rewrite — resolve_spawn_params is the same code, just named and bounded.
endorsed.reason:
The 740-line monolith is real and the proposal is sound, but the effort estimate is too optimistic. Here is what the code actually shows:

CONFIRMED: run_or_prewarm (lines 590-1329) is a sequential monolith with zero intermediate named stages. The 14-param signature, the Clippy suppress, and the dense block of validation → config → model-pin → effort → permission → workspace-5-way → trust → MCP-provision → full-config-flag → attachments → CLI-caps-probe → command-build (200+ lines) → env-injection (api-key/local-llm/nothink) → effort-flag → SpawnKey assembly → dispatch-branch are all literally inlined. Reading any one concern requires skimming all the others.

WHY AGREE: The proposed split — a `SpawnParams` struct populated by `resolve_spawn_params()`, leaving `run_or_prewarm` as ~80-line orchestration — is the minimal, correct decomposition. It matches the single conceptual seam that already exists in the code (everything before line 1309 *prepares* the spawn; everything from 1309 on *executes* it). The public API (`assistant_send` / `assistant_prewarm`) is unchanged. The two shim callers just pass `prewarm: bool`, so no call-site rewrite is needed. `SpawnParams` has a natural home in warm_pool.rs or a new params.rs — it even has a partial analogue already in `warm_pool::SpawnKey` (the fingerprint struct built at line 1291).

WHAT THE PROPOSAL UNDERESTIMATES: `resolve_spawn_params` must return not just the listed fields but also `_mcp_guard` (the RAII drop guard that keeps the temp MCP config file alive), `user_line` (the pre-built stdin payload), `cmd` (the already-configured `tokio::process::Command`), and the `window_label` string. `cmd` in particular is built across ~200 lines with interleaved branching on model/use_full_config/prompting_mode/local_llm/api_key/caps — that branching can't be collapsed, it just moves into the new function. So the return type is a non-trivial struct with a `Command` (not `Clone`), a guard, and a `Vec<u8>`. Rust's ownership model means `cmd` cannot live in a plain struct without careful lifetime design, and `Command` is `!Clone`, so `SpawnParams` has to own it or the fn must return a tuple. That's solvable but it adds ~30 min of type-wrangling the proposal doesn't account for.

EFFORT REALITY: The code is dense but self-contained. There are no cross-module side effects hidden in the monolith — the helper calls (`write_mcp_config`, `clamp_effort`, `CliCaps::active`, etc.) are already bounded. A careful engineer can: (1) define `SpawnParams` / `ResolvedSpawn` with all owned fields including `cmd`, (2) lift the resolution body into `resolve_spawn_params`, (3) reduce `run_or_prewarm` to the three-line orchestration, (4) fix the borrow checker fallout (mostly the `_mcp_guard` lifetime and the `model` string that gets passed to both the key and `dispatch_turn`). Estimated wall-clock: 3-5 hours for someone who knows the file, plus a full `cargo check` clean pass. That is solidly medium on a well-understood codebase — the proposal's 'medium' label is accurate, though at the upper end.

NOT A CURE WORSE THAN THE DISEASE: There is no behavioral risk here. The refactor touches zero public commands, zero Tauri event names, zero SpawnKey fields, and zero warm-pool logic. The only risk is a Rust type error during the extraction (owned `Command` in struct, `_mcp_guard` lifetime) — both are straightforward to resolve and `cargo check` is the gatekeeper. The reward — being able to read the resolution logic without wading through 700 lines of interleaved concerns — is high given how often this file is touched (it is the hottest file in the backend).

endorsed.title: tree_kill is implemented twice, identically, in oneshot.rs and warm_pool.rs
endorsed.symptom: oneshot.rs defines a private fn tree_kill(pid) (lines 81-102) that does taskkill /F /T /PID on Windows, kill -TERM on Unix. warm_pool.rs defines pub(super) fn kill_child_tree(pid) (lines 54-74) with byte-for-byte identical logic. oneshot.rs can't use warm_pool's version because warm_pool is pub(super) to assistant — i.e. both are in the same module tree. The duplication means any future change (e.g., adding /T to the Unix path, or CREATE_NO_WINDOW on the kill path) must happen in both files. The names even differ (tree_kill vs kill_child_tree).
endorsed.recommendation: Delete oneshot.rs::tree_kill entirely and replace its 3 call-sites (lines 113, 124, and kill_all_enhance_children) with super::warm_pool::kill_child_tree(pid). No API change, no new abstraction — just remove the copy. If the name inconsistency bothers, rename warm_pool's to kill_child_tree_by_pid in a follow-up. One-line change per call-site.
endorsed.reason: Duplication confirmed byte-for-byte. `turn.rs` already imports `warm_pool::kill_child_tree` (line 19) — the consolidation pattern is established and proven in the same module. `oneshot.rs` simply never followed suit. Fix: add `use super::warm_pool::kill_child_tree;` to oneshot.rs, delete the local `fn tree_kill` (lines 81-102), replace three call-sites (lines 113, 123, 314 — the proposal undercounts; there are three, not two). The `pid == 0` guard in oneshot's version is non-load-bearing (pids only stored after a successful spawn). Risk is near-zero: identical logic, visibility already correct (`pub(super)` reaches siblings), no new abstraction introduced.

endorsed.title: Three giant system-prompt strings (14KB combined) live in turn.rs, hardcoded
endorsed.symptom: RIFT_SYSTEM_ADDENDUM_TOOLS (6354 chars), RIFT_SYSTEM_ADDENDUM_LOCAL (7577 chars), and RIFT_SYSTEM_ADDENDUM_NO_WS (~300 chars) are 14KB of product copy embedded as raw Rust string constants in the turn engine. They are not executable logic — they are text content that changes on its own schedule (product iterations, wording tweaks, new tool names). Because they're in turn.rs, every edit to the prompt requires touching the 2700-line hot file, recompiling the whole binary, and losing the ability to do A/B or per-user overrides. RIFT_SYSTEM_ADDENDUM_LOCAL (local-LLM) is especially volatile — it carries extensive behavioral instructions likely to need iteration. The SpawnKey uses addendum_ptr (a raw pointer comparison as a fingerprint) specifically because the strings are static constants, which is a code smell: the key encoding is coupled to the storage representation.
endorsed.recommendation: Move the three constants to a dedicated src-tauri/src/assistant/system_prompts.rs. Replace the addendum_ptr field in SpawnKey with an enum AddendumVariant { Tools, NoWorkspace, Local } (3 variants, trivially PartialEq). This eliminates the pointer-as-fingerprint hack and gives the prompts their own file where product writers can find them. The 'move to an external file loaded at runtime' option is a separate upgrade that's only worth it if prompt iteration velocity is actually high — don't do that without a concrete need.
endorsed.reason: The restructure is sound on two independent grounds. First, the `addendum_ptr: usize` field in `SpawnKey` (warm_pool.rs:128) is a real smell: `SpawnKey` derives `PartialEq` and the equality of `addendum_ptr` depends on the linker assigning distinct static addresses to three different string literals — a property the compiler guarantees today but that is not part of the language contract and is invisible to any future reader who sees a `usize` field in a `PartialEq` struct. A 3-variant enum (`AddendumVariant { Tools, NoWorkspace, Local }`) is the semantically correct type, makes the intent explicit, and costs nothing. Second, the 14KB of product-copy strings are logically independent of the turn engine: they carry behavioral instructions for the assistant, not spawn/stream logic, and RIFT_SYSTEM_ADDENDUM_LOCAL in particular already has its own multi-line explanatory comment block treating it as a separate concern. Putting them in their own file (`system_prompts.rs`) follows the project's own module-per-concern pattern (see `mcp_server.rs`, `git_local.rs`, `bridge.rs` as peers). The single-line constraint (CVE-2024-24576) is preserved — it's a string-content requirement, not a file-location requirement. The 'move to runtime-loaded files' extension is correctly deferred; the proposal is the minimal structural fix. The effort estimate of 'small' is accurate: new file with 3 consts + trivial enum + one field type change + update the one construction site at turn.rs:1302. No behavior changes, no protocol changes, no test surface affected.

endorsed.title: mod.rs owns substantial non-glue logic: MCP config write, DACL lockdown, seq counter, RAII guard
endorsed.symptom: mod.rs is supposed to be a re-export hub (the R1-R8 split comments make this intent explicit). But lines 126-324 implement real business logic: a process-lifetime AtomicU64 nonce counter, a McpConfigGuard RAII struct with Drop impl, write_mcp_config (a 160-line fn that builds JSON, manages the per-turn filename race via the nonce, does async icacls ACL lockdown on a detached thread), and cleanup_mcp_config_on_exit. This logic is called from turn.rs and oneshot.rs but lives in mod.rs. Finding 'where does MCP config file management live?' requires knowing to look in mod.rs, not in a dedicated file. The icacls ACL logic is also duplicated between write_mcp_config (mod.rs:244-286) and config.rs's harden_config_acl (lines 95-124) — same CREATE_NO_WINDOW pattern, same detached thread, same icacls args.
endorsed.recommendation: Move McpConfigGuard, MCP_CFG_SEQ, write_mcp_config, and cleanup_mcp_config_on_exit into a new mcp_config.rs (or into the existing mcp_bridge.rs if the scope fits). Extract the DACL icacls logic into a single shared fn harden_file_acl(path: &Path) in a security.rs or inline into the one caller. mod.rs becomes a pure re-export hub as intended. Medium effort because write_mcp_config has callers in both turn.rs and oneshot.rs and the pub visibility needs adjusting.
endorsed.reason: The finding is accurate and the restructure is worth it. mod.rs is 359 lines, ~200 of which (55%) are non-glue business logic — McpConfigGuard, MCP_CFG_SEQ, write_mcp_config (160L), cleanup_mcp_config_on_exit — sitting in a file whose R1-R8 comment block explicitly declares it a re-export hub. That contradiction is the exact kind of implicit coupling that makes "where does per-turn MCP config file management live?" a grep problem rather than an obvious answer. The icacls duplication is real: mod.rs:244-286 and config.rs:95-124 are structurally identical spawn blocks; mod.rs already delegates acl_principal to config.rs, so merging the spawn into a shared harden_file_acl in config.rs is a clean deduplication with no behavior change. Mechanical risk is low: write_mcp_config is private (fn, not pub), McpConfigGuard is private (struct), both already consumed via use super:: in turn.rs and oneshot.rs. Moving them to a new mcp_config.rs requires adjusting those two use lines plus one pub use in mod.rs (or one call-path update in lib.rs for cleanup_mcp_config_on_exit). No logic changes, no new abstractions. The "medium" label is slightly generous — the actual work is closer to small (new file + 3-4 import adjustments + merge the icacls block). The one structural nuance: mcp_bridge.rs already exists for MCP child-side concerns, so a new mcp_config.rs adds a third MCP-adjacent file, but that is still unambiguously better than the current mod.rs burial. Worth doing on the next maintenance pass.

endorsed.title: run_or_prewarm boolean-flag dispatch fuses two distinct entry points
endorsed.symptom: A single 700-line async function (run_or_prewarm) serves two structurally different operations — a real turn dispatch and a prewarm spare spawn — unified by a `prewarm: bool` flag. The prewarm path executes ~650 lines of shared cmd-build machinery (model resolution, SpawnKey construction, MCP config, argv assembly) and then early-returns via `if prewarm { return prewarm_spawn(...) }` at line 1309, never touching the user-line or dispatch path. The send path falls through to dispatch_turn/cold_spawn_and_run. These two callers (assistant_send and assistant_prewarm) share ONLY the cmd-build logic, which accounts for roughly 650 of those 700 lines — the actual dispatch logic is completely disjoint.
endorsed.recommendation: Extract the shared argv/cmd construction (~lines 600–1303) into a private `build_cmd(...)` helper returning `(SpawnKey, Command, McpConfigGuard)`. assistant_send calls build_cmd → dispatch_turn directly. assistant_prewarm calls build_cmd → prewarm_spawn directly. Eliminates the bool param, removes the dead `user_line` assembly path from prewarm, and makes each entry point ~30 lines. Effort is mechanical: the shared block has no branches that depend on `prewarm`, so extraction is a pure refactor. Worth doing before the next extension of this path.
endorsed.reason:
The structural claim is accurate. run_or_prewarm (lines 590–1329, ~740 lines) has exactly one branch on `prewarm` — a single early-return at line 1309 — and zero other `prewarm`-conditional branches in the preceding 700 lines of cmd-building. The two call sites (assistant_send/assistant_prewarm) are semantically disjoint: one delivers a real turn with a user_line, the other parks a warm child. The shared block builds the full argv machinery (model resolution, Fable/Haiku guards, SpawnKey, MCP config, capability gating, effort mapping, nothink shim, tool allowlists) identically for both paths.

Two concrete correctness/cleanliness issues the proposal correctly identifies: (1) `user_line` (line 1284, building a JSON user-envelope from `String::new()`) is assembled on the prewarm path and then silently discarded — `prewarm_spawn` receives `cmd`, not `user_line`. Pure waste. (2) The session-pin side effects (`save_session_cwd`, `save_session_model`, lines 751–761) fire on the prewarm path; they're intentional in behaviour but are buried in cmd-build machinery where they're easy to miss.

The extraction is genuinely mechanical. The shared block has no logic to unpick — no `if prewarm` switches, no conditional accumulation. The main engineering decision is the signature: `build_cmd` needs to return `(SpawnKey, Command, Option<McpConfigGuard>, String /* resolved model */)` because the resolved model is consumed by both `prewarm_spawn` and `dispatch_turn`. A `BuildCmdOut` struct avoids returning a 4-tuple. The ~12 input params warrant a `BuildCmdArgs` struct too, or a subset can collapse (several are already resolved inside).

Effort is realistically small-to-medium, not medium. There are no behavioral branches to unpick, no tests to rewrite (the warm-pool integration and streaming tests verify the paths that matter and would catch regressions). The risk is mechanical correctness on one large extraction — low for a senior Rust engineer, not zero for an unfamiliar contributor.

Worth doing: yes. This is one of the cleaner refactors possible on turn.rs — it removes a false unity between two structurally different operations, eliminates a silently-discarded allocation on the prewarm path, and makes each entry point's intent obvious in ~30 lines instead of requiring the reader to understand 700 lines of shared context before seeing the branch point. On a shipping product with active extension work on this path (re-warm support was added 2026-06-28 per the comments), the restructure reduces the chance that a future caller misunderstands which parts of the shared block apply to their path.

endorsed.title: Four inter-locking spare-detection booleans inside run_turn_loop
endorsed.symptom: The persistent reader loop carries four flags that exist solely to distinguish 'I was spawned as a prewarm spare with no first turn' from 'I was spawned by a real send with a first turn in hand': `has_inhand_first` (line 1835), `cold_first` (1836), `first_turn_flag` (1837), and `spare_first_adopt` (1873). These flags were accreted when the prewarm path was grafted onto a loop designed for regular cold spawns. `cold_first` feeds into `emit_turn_end_error`; `first_turn_flag` gates which `turn_start` timestamp to use; `spare_first_adopt` gates the silent-cold-retry branch for a dead spare (lines 1956-1963). Three of these four are only ever true on the very first iteration of the loop.
endorsed.recommendation: Consolidate into a single `SpawnKind` enum stored in RunCtx: `enum SpawnKind { RealFirst { turn_start: Instant }, PrewarmSpare }`. Replace all four flags with pattern-matching on it. The prewarm-spare Eof branch reads `matches!(ctx.spawn_kind, SpawnKind::PrewarmSpare) && !handshake_done` (one condition, no separate flag). The cold_first / first_turn_flag timing logic also collapses: `if let SpawnKind::RealFirst { turn_start } = ctx.spawn_kind`. Eliminates conceptual duplication without changing behavior.
endorsed.reason:
The four flags genuinely encode one binary fact — "was I spawned as a prewarm spare with no in-hand first turn?" — and the current code already has `first_turn: Option<TurnCmd>` in `RunCtx` that directly captures that same fact. The proposed `SpawnKind` enum is essentially a rename+move of what `ctx.first_turn.is_some()` already tells you.

Concretely:
- `has_inhand_first` = `ctx.first_turn.is_some()` (computable from existing field, no new state needed)
- `cold_first` and `first_turn_flag` are both `ctx.is_first_turn && ctx.first_turn.is_some()` — identical expressions, and `ctx.is_first_turn` is always `true` for the prewarm spawn path (line 1707 hardcodes it), making `cold_first == first_turn_flag == ctx.first_turn.is_some()` in the prewarm case
- `spare_first_adopt` = `ctx.first_turn.is_none() && !handshake_done`

Three of the four flags could be eliminated without adding any new type — just read `ctx.first_turn.is_some()`/`is_none()` inline. The `SpawnKind` enum is slightly nicer than that but also slightly more than necessary.

The one genuine risk is `cold_first` passed to `emit_turn_end_error`: that function uses `is_first_turn` to gate the `--resume` session-lost branch (line 2424). That logic is correct and the flag correctly holds `false` when the spare adopts a warm reuse turn. Any refactor must preserve that: `emit_turn_end_error(..., ctx.first_turn.is_some() && ctx.is_first_turn, ...)` is the drop-in.

The restructure is worth doing: the duplication is real, the comments across four flag definitions are load-bearing documentation for a single invariant, and the mismatch between `cold_first` and `first_turn_flag` being identical-but-named differently is a latent confusion trap for future work on this loop. Effort is small — all changes live inside `run_turn_loop` (lines 1835–1873) and one call site for `emit_turn_end_error`. No API or public interface changes. The `SpawnKind` enum is optional sugar; the minimal fix is just deleting the four locals and substituting `ctx.first_turn.is_some()`/`is_none()` directly.

endorsed.title: FE prewarm.ts dual-debounce logic adds conditional complexity to a simple trigger
endorsed.symptom: prewarm.ts has two debounce constants (PREWARM_FIRST_FIRE_MS=150, PREWARM_DEBOUNCE_MS=600) and a conditional at line 106 that picks between them based on `isFirstTurn && lastFiredKey === null`. The dual-constant logic is a small but real accretion: the 150ms path was added (per the comment) to solve 'fast typer beats the 600ms window'. The condition mixes two orthogonal concerns — 'is this a fresh tab' and 'has a prior fire latched' — into a single boolean expression. The module is small enough that this isn't a maintenance burden, but the condition is subtler than it looks.
endorsed.recommendation: Add a `lastFiredKey === null` inline comment: 'also fires post-tab-switch re-arms; intentional — a just-switched tab is equally cold.' No code change needed unless the behavior is wrong. Low urgency.
endorsed.reason: The condition at line 106 has a genuine documentation gap: `lastFiredKey === null` silently covers the post-tab-switch re-arm case, but the surrounding comment (lines 103-105) only describes the "no prior fire" interpretation. A reader debugging a "why did the fast path fire here?" question would miss that. The proposed fix — one inline comment, no code change — is exactly right in scope. The behavior itself is defensible (a just-switched tab is as cold as a fresh one), the two constants are well-named, and the module is small enough that there's no refactor payoff. Worth doing purely as a comment addition: literally one line, zero risk, real future-maintainer value.

endorsed.title: PathFilter compiled from env on every tool call, not once at startup
endorsed.symptom: `PathFilter::from_env()` is called independently at the start of each of the three file-access tools, which means `std::env::var(RIFT_MCP_INCLUDE/EXCLUDE)` is read + `compile_globs` (which calls `glob_to_regex` → `regex::Regex::new` per pattern) runs three times per compound model action that calls read, list, and grep in sequence. The env vars are set once at spawn and never change, so this is wasted regex compilation on every call. For a project with a non-trivial include/exclude list this adds measurable latency that the user experiences as the assistant feeling 'slow'.
endorsed.recommendation: Move `let filter = PathFilter::from_env();` into `run_stdio` alongside `let roots = load_roots()`, then pass it as a param to `handle_request` → tool fns (same pattern already used for `roots`). Regex compilation happens once at MCP-child boot instead of per-call. One-line change to `run_stdio`, minimal signature change to the three tool fns.
endorsed.reason: Evidence confirmed. `PathFilter::from_env()` is called at L279, L329, and L432 — once per tool-fn invocation, independent of each other. Each call reads two env vars and runs `compile_globs` → `glob_to_regex` → `regex::Regex::new` per pattern. Env vars are set once at MCP-child spawn and never change, so all re-reads are purely redundant. The existing `roots` vec already demonstrates the correct pattern: computed once in `run_stdio` (L859), passed through `handle_request` as `&[PathBuf]`, forwarded to each tool fn. The fix is a direct copy of that pattern: add `filter: &PathFilter` to `handle_request` and the three tool fns, compute once in `run_stdio`. Signature change is mechanical — only internal callers, no public API surface, tests use `from_globs` not `from_env` so they're unaffected. The "slow" complaint is plausible here: regex NFA compilation is not free, and a project with 5-10 include/exclude globs fires 6 compilations per compound model action (read+list+grep across two env vars). No intentional design rationale justifies per-call recompilation over a constant. Risk is near-zero on a shipping product.

endorsed.title: strip_unc / strip_verbatim duplicated between mcp_server.rs and git_local.rs
endorsed.symptom: Two separate cfg-gated `#[cfg(windows)]` / `#[cfg(not(windows))]` fn pairs exist that do the identical job: strip the `\\?\` verbatim UNC prefix from a `Path`. `mcp_server.rs` calls its copy `strip_unc`; `git_local.rs` calls its copy `strip_verbatim`. The comment in git_local.rs explicitly acknowledges this: 'Mirrors `strip_unc` in mcp_server.rs (kept local — git tools don't import across that boundary).' The boundary justification is weak: both files are `pub(crate)` siblings in the same `assistant` module, so the fn is easily shareable.
endorsed.recommendation: Add a single `pub(super) fn strip_unc(p: &Path) -> PathBuf` to mod.rs (or a small `path_util.rs`), and have both files use it. The 'no cross-boundary import' concern in the comment is a self-imposed fiction — they're in the same module already. This also eliminates the name inconsistency (unc vs verbatim).
endorsed.reason: The duplication is real and the justification comment is self-contradictory. Both `mcp_server.rs` and `git_local.rs` are `pub mod` siblings declared in the same `assistant/mod.rs` (lines 22 and 24). The "don't import across that boundary" comment in `git_local.rs` L55 invents a boundary that doesn't exist — they share a crate module namespace and can freely call `super::` or a shared sibling. The two implementations are functionally identical (same `\\?\` strip, same non-Windows no-op), diverging only in name (`strip_unc` vs `strip_verbatim`) and if-let vs match style. A single `pub(super) fn strip_unc` in `mod.rs` (or a 10-line `path_util.rs` sub-module) eliminates the copy, the name inconsistency, and the misleading comment. On a mature shipping codebase, the usual "don't churn" argument applies to behaviour changes; a pure refactor of two private 6-line fns with zero public surface carries essentially no risk. The effort is genuinely small: move one fn pair, update two call sites, delete the other fn pair, delete the comment.

endorsed.title: Local `dunce` shim module is vestigial dead weight
endorsed.symptom: mcp_server.rs contains a `mod dunce` that wraps `std::fs::canonicalize` with no additional behaviour — the shim is 8 lines to do nothing. The comment explains it exists so future code could override canonicalize, but the real `dunce` crate (which strips UNC and is already referenced by name in the comment) is explicitly not used 'because we already handle that in `strip_unc`'. The result is an indirection layer named after a crate it isn't, with a fake override surface that nothing actually uses.
endorsed.recommendation: Delete the `mod dunce` block and replace the one call site (`load_roots`, L83) with `std::fs::canonicalize(s).ok()`. If the real `dunce` crate is ever wanted, add it as a proper Cargo dep. The current shim adds noise and false-signals 'there's something non-standard happening here' to every reader.
endorsed.reason: The shim is confirmed dead weight. The comment at L242-245 openly admits it's a placeholder ("for now it's std::fs::canonicalize"), the override surface is never exercised, and the module name actively misleads readers into expecting UNC-stripping behavior that isn't there. The "future deferred logic" argument doesn't hold — if the real dunce crate is ever needed it gets added as a proper Cargo dep in seconds, not rescued from this shadow module. The fix is one block deletion + one substitution at L83; zero behavior change, zero test churn.

endorsed.title: Bridge TCP protocol is a correct but slightly leaky abstraction — raw TCP for a fire-once RPC is visible through the seams
endorsed.symptom: The loopback TCP bridge is structurally sound (token auth, per-connection close after one authed dispatch, both sides capped, timeouts, RAII guard for registry) and the rationale is well-grounded: the MCP child is a separate process with no Tauri handle, so process-boundary IPC is genuinely required. The leak is cosmetic but real: `mcp_bridge::bridge_call_inner` re-reads `RIFT_BRIDGE_PORT` and `RIFT_BRIDGE_TOKEN` from env on every call even though those values are static for the process lifetime. More visibly, the TCP `connect → write → read → close` cycle for `notify` (fire-and-forget) incurs the same TCP handshake overhead as the long-parking `ask_user` call — there's no lightweight 'send only' path even though two of the three ops don't need a data response, only an ack.
